fullDescription: Cinematic camera motion over the user's own draft screenshot - floating device, perspective push, desk scene - for launch posts and teasers. Camera-only discipline keeps the video model from redrawing the interface: the design is composited into a plate first, then animated with one modest move and a locked-UI clause. Adapted from rediumvex's ai-video-generator-claude and Krea's krea-marketing (both MIT).
prompt:
# UI Fly-Through

Generative video wants to redraw your interface; this skill is about never letting it. The deliverable is cinematic camera motion over the user's own design - a Superdesign draft screenshot placed into a scene and flown past, orbited, or pushed toward - for launch posts and teasers. The design already exists and is already right. The video's only job is to add depth, light, and a camera; the moment it is allowed to touch the interface itself, every label it redraws comes back wrong.

`Video Generation / Billboard Placement` warns that video models fight UI screenshots. That warning stands. This skill is the disciplined exception, and it holds only inside strict limits: the camera moves, the interface does not, and nobody is asked to read anything.

## When to use

- A finished draft needs a launch or teaser asset that shows the actual product, not an abstraction.
- A social post wants the interface with depth and polish - a floating device, a lit desk, a slow push.
- The user asks for a "product video", "app showcase", or "demo clip" where the motion is atmosphere, not instruction.

Do not use for: a walkthrough the viewer must read or follow (record the real screen; generative video cannot hold legible small text through a scene change), the brand mark placed in the world (use `Video Generation / Billboard Placement`), an ambient background behind a headline (use `Video Generation / Hero Loop`), or in-product UI motion (that belongs in CSS, not in a video file).

## Why camera-only is the whole trick

Rendered text survives a camera move and dies in a scene change. This is a verified behavior, not a preference: a frame containing dense real text, animated with a pure camera-only move and the instruction that nothing else changes, stays legible through the last frame - while the same frame under motion that alters the scene (elements animating, objects entering, light shifting) drifts progressively, and the drift lands on the smallest type first.

So the discipline is absolute:

- **Never ask the UI to be alive.** No "data flows", no "charts animate", no "notifications slide in", no cursor, no scrolling, no screen transitions. Each of those is an instruction to redraw the interface, and a redrawn interface is a deformed one.
- **One camera move per clip**, modest and complete: an orbit of `10–15°`, a push that covers a fraction of the frame, a lateral drift. No whip pans, no fast zooms, no move that becomes another move.
- **Accept what the shot is.** Small text reads as texture at these sizes; the clip sells depth, materiality, and confidence. If the brief needs the viewer to read the interface, this is the wrong tool.
- **The UI stays sharpest inside a scene.** A screenshot filling the frame edge-to-edge gives the model nothing to do except reinterpret pixels. A screen at `50–70%` of frame, angled in an environment, gives the camera something real to move through and keeps the interface a photographed object rather than a canvas.

## Shot menu

Pick one and commit.

| Shot | What moves | What stays locked | Reads as |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Floating device** - the design on a slab or laptop at a slight angle in a dark void, rim-lit, soft reflection below | Camera orbits `10–15°`, shallow depth of field | Device position, screen content, light setup | Premium, product-first |
| **Perspective push** - camera pushes toward the screen plane, stopping just before it fills the frame | Camera travels forward at constant speed | Screen content, framing endpoint chosen so UI never goes edge-to-edge | Confident, immersive |
| **Desk scene** - device in a real workspace at dusk, warm ambient light, props in bokeh | Camera drifts laterally or pushes gently | Screen content, environment layout | Credible, human-scale |
| **Side glide** - two or three screens of the same design system in an angled row | Camera dollies along the row with parallax | Every screen's content, the row's geometry | System-level, "this is a whole product" |

The perspective push is the highest-risk shot: the closer the screen gets to filling the frame, the more the model is tempted to reinterpret it. End the move with visible scene around the screen.

## Two stages, always

The same plate-then-animate doctrine as `Video Generation / Billboard Placement`: there is a still in between, and the composition is won there.

**Stage 1 - build the plate with image generation.** Attach the actual draft screenshot as a reference image and generate the scene around it: the device slab, the desk, the angled row. Nano Banana 2 (`10` credits, up to 10 reference images) is the default for this compositing. The image prompt describes scene, light, and camera position only - never the interface's contents. Do not name the product, quote its headline, or describe what is on screen; the reference is the source of truth, and describing it is an invitation to redraw it. Inspect the plate at full size before animating: every label legible, screen edges straight, no invented UI elements. Do not spend video credits on a plate that has already drifted.

**Stage 2 - animate the camera.** Feed the plate to video generation and describe motion only.

## Motion budget

The motion prompt is capped at **500 characters**. Order:

1. **Camera** - the one move, its direction, its extent, its speed.
2. **Environment life** - light behavior, reflection, bokeh drift. Sparingly; this shot needs less street life than a billboard.
3. **The lock** - "the screen content stays exactly as it is: it does not change, redraw, animate, or scroll." This clause is never cut, whatever else the character budget costs.

Name the speed as `steady`, `constant`, `natural realtime`. Do not write `slow`, `gentle`, or `soft` - video models literalize those words into slow motion, which reads as heavy and dated on a product shot. (An ambient hero loop wants near-stillness; a fly-through wants one real move at natural speed. Different deliverables, different vocabulary.)

A fly-through wants `4–6` seconds. The move should complete with a beat to spare; a cut-off move reads as an error.

## Model and resolution

| Model | Role | Credits per 5s (480p / 720p / 1080p) |
|---|---|---|
| Seedance Fast | Trial pass - confirm the move and the lock | 15 / 20 / 45 |
| Seedance Pro | The finish default - smoothest camera motion | 25 / 50 / 120 |
| Hailuo | Only when the brand wants visible energy | 30 / 30 / 50 (6s) |

**Always run the trial first: Seedance Fast at 480p, 15 credits.** A trial exists to answer two questions cheaply - does the move land, and does the interface hold? Only then spend on the finish. State the plate cost, the trial cost, and the finish cost together when proposing the shot, and get agreement on the ladder, not on one number: a typical run is `10` (plate) + `15` (trial) + `50` (Seedance Pro 720p finish).

## Prompt skeleton

```text
Steady <orbit right about 12 degrees | push toward the screen | lateral dolly along the row>, one continuous move at constant natural speed, completing with a short hold. <Rim light holds steady | reflections shift subtly on the desk surface | background bokeh drifts>. The screen content stays exactly as it is: it does not change, redraw, animate, or scroll, and every straight edge of the device stays straight. No added text, letters, logos, watermarks, or UI elements. No cursor.
```

Count the characters before sending. If it exceeds 500, cut the environment clause first - never the lock.

## Reject a clip when

- Any label shimmers, re-renders, or grows pseudo-characters. Compare the last frame to the first at full size - drift is progressive, so the last frame is where it shows.
- A straight edge bends: device bezels, screen borders, or card boundaries warping as the camera moves.
- The interface animates - anything scrolls, populates, flips, or lights up that was static in the plate.
- The move overshoots: a `15°` orbit that became `40°`, a push that swallowed the screen edge-to-edge.
- A second move appears - the push that develops a pan, the orbit that starts tilting.
- The screen's glow flickers or the reflection detaches from the device.
- New UI, text, or icons appear anywhere in the scene.
- It only works because nobody looks closely. This asset sits on a launch post; someone will look closely.

Watch it at full size before delivering, and check the last frame against the plate specifically. A clip that survives that comparison is a launch asset; one that does not is a retake, not a note.

---

Shot geometry adapted from [ai-video-generator-claude](https://github.com/rediumvex/ai-video-generator-claude) by @rediumvex, MIT licensed. Camera-only text-survival discipline informed by [krea-marketing](https://github.com/krea-ai/skills) by Krea, MIT licensed.

Rewritten for Superdesign: built as a two-stage plate-then-animate workflow over the user's own draft screenshot, compressed to the 500-character motion prompt and the model/credit ladder, and the source's live-UI animation guidance ("elements animate, data flows") deliberately inverted into a camera-only lock - on-screen motion is exactly what makes video models redraw an interface.
